hardinessNote: Very hardy Northern Lights series azalea; flowering buds can still be damaged by late frost.
visual: Rounded, deciduous shrub with spring trusses of creamy yellow to pale ivory trumpet flowers, strongly yellow-blotched on the upper petals and lightly fragrant. Green foliage can take warm autumn tones.
pest: Vine weevil, lacebugs, aphids and caterpillars; petal blight, powdery mildew and Phytophthora in unsuitable conditions.
aspect: East or North; part shade with morning sun; can tolerate more sun where roots remain cool and moist.
soil: Humus-rich, consistently moist but free-draining acidic soil, ideally pH about 4.5–6.
soilWarning: Avoid chalky or alkaline ground, waterlogging and drying out. Use ericaceous compost and rainwater where necessary.
water: Water regularly in the first two seasons; irrigate during dry spring and summer weather, preferably with rainwater.
prune: Little pruning required; remove dead wood and lightly shape immediately after flowering to preserve next year’s buds.
toxicity: Harmful if eaten to people and pets; all azalea and rhododendron parts can be toxic.
cvs: University of Minnesota Northern Lights breeding programme; sold as Northern Hi-Lights / Northern Hi-lights.
resilience: Exceptional cold hardiness, but roots dislike drought and alkalinity.
uses: Acid-loving shrub borders, woodland edges, ericaceous beds and large acid-soil containers.
pollination: Attractive to bumblebees and other spring pollinators when open.
uncertain: Relative scores and some seasonal details are horticultural estimates.

hardinessNote: A genus-only entry. Hardiness varies considerably with species and cultivar; do not assign a single rating to an unidentified Daphne.
height: Variable; approximately 0.3–2.5 m for commonly sold shrubs
visual: Usually a compact to upright shrub with narrow leathery or soft green leaves and small, richly fragrant pink, white or yellow flowers. Some daphnes remain evergreen; others are deciduous.
pest: Occasional aphids, scale and fungal leaf spot; sudden decline and Phytophthora root rot are more consequential than insect pests.
aspect: Sheltered East or West position; light shade or morning sun for many species, though requirements vary.
soil: Deep, humus-rich, moisture-retentive but freely draining soil, often neutral to slightly alkaline.
soilWarning: Do not allow waterlogging or severe drying; daphnes strongly resent root disturbance and transplanting. Some species have different pH preferences.
water: Keep evenly moist through establishment, then water during long dry spells; never leave the roots standing in water.
prune: Avoid routine pruning. If essential, remove individual damaged stems sparingly after flowering.
toxicity: TOXIC if eaten; sap can irritate skin. Keep away from children and pets and wear gloves.
cvs: Species and cultivar were not supplied; this is a provisional genus-level entry only.
resilience: Many are cold hardy in sheltered ground, but intolerance of waterlogged roots and disturbance is common.
uses: Scented path edges, doorway plantings, sheltered mixed shrub borders and sensory gardens.
foliage: evergreen / semi-evergreen / deciduous depending on species
rootSize: Often deep, sensitive roots; dislikes transplanting.
stockForm: Variable small to medium fragrant shrub.
pollination: Fragrant flowers attract early-flying insects; varies by species.
uncertain: ESSENTIAL: exact Daphne species or cultivar is missing; all size, season, hardiness and care fields are genus-level guidance, not cultivar data.
Replace this placeholder when a plant label or photograph becomes available.

hardinessNote: RHS rates this Knap Hill/Exbury azalea H6; shelter flower buds from exposed late-frost pockets.
visual: Deciduous azalea with orange-red buds opening into generous trusses of fragrant golden-orange and nectar-yellow funnel-shaped flowers; fresh young leaves may be bronze-flushed.
pest: Vine weevil, lacebug, aphids and leafhopper; powdery mildew, bud blast and Phytophthora root rot.
aspect: Sheltered East, West or South; bright dappled light to part shade.
soil: Moist but well-drained, organic-rich, distinctly acidic soil.
soilWarning: Not suited to chalky or alkaline soil. Avoid summer drought, stagnant water and strongly drying winds.
water: Maintain even moisture while establishing and during dry weather. Rainwater preferable on alkaline mains water.
prune: Only lightly prune just after flowering if necessary; remove dead or damaged branches.
toxicity: Harmful if eaten; toxic to dogs, cats and other pets.
cvs: A Knap Hill/Exbury deciduous azalea. The word Sunte Nectarine is a Rhododendron cultivar, not Daphne.
resilience: Winter-hardy and showy but dependent on acid soil and steady moisture.
uses: Spring shrub borders, acid-loving planting schemes, woodland margins and large ericaceous tubs.
pollination: Nectar and pollen accessible to early-season insects.
uncertain: Peak month shifts with local conditions; numerical ratings are estimates.

hardinessNote: Root hardy in much of the UK; foliage generally dies back in cold winters.
visual: Architectural clump of long, deeply lobed dark-green leaves splashed and marbled creamy white, topped by tall vertical flower spikes with white flowers and purplish hoods.
pest: Occasional slugs or snails on young leaves; powdery mildew in dry or crowded positions.
aspect: Sheltered East, South or West; sun or partial shade.
soil: Deep, fertile, well-drained loam; tolerates chalk and many other soil textures.
soilWarning: Winter wet and poor drainage can rot the crown; white-variegated leaves can scorch in hot sun.
water: Water during establishment and prolonged drought; once established, moderately drought tolerant.
prune: Cut finished flower stems to the base and remove dead foliage in late winter or early spring.
toxicity: Not commonly classified as seriously poisonous; avoid consumption and wear gloves for skin sensitivity.
cvs: Corrects the incomplete label White Wate to Acanthus Whitewater.
resilience: Bold perennial with drought tolerance once rooted; can regrow from fleshy roots.
uses: Architectural borders, Mediterranean-style schemes, foliage contrast and cut flower spikes.
rootSize: Deep, vigorous fleshy roots; root fragments may reshoot.
pollination: Flowers can attract bumblebees and other insect visitors.
uncertain: Acanthus Whitewater is the likely interpretation of White Wate.

hardinessNote: RHS H5; shelter new shoots from late frosts and cold drying winds.
visual: Vigorous self-clinging deciduous climber with oval, serrated dark-green foliage and airy, flattened creamy-white lacecap-like flower clusters with conspicuous sterile floral bracts.
pest: Aphids, capsid bugs, scale, vine weevil; occasional leaf spots and powdery mildew.
aspect: Sheltered North, East, West or partly sunny South wall; sun or partial shade.
soil: Moisture-retentive, humus-rich but well-drained loam or improved clay; adaptable pH.
soilWarning: Allow ample support area and avoid dry wall-foot soil. Aerial roots can attach to masonry, trees or other structures.
water: Deeply water new plants and roots by warm walls; water in prolonged drought once established.
prune: After flowering remove unwanted lateral growth and congested stems; do not heavily prune unless necessary.
toxicity: RHS flags possible skin allergen and harmful effects if eaten by pets; wear gloves.
cvs: 'Windmills' is also associated with Schizophragma fauriei / Hydrangea fauriei 'Plooster' in horticultural naming; RHS currently records this name as a synonym.
resilience: Hardy climbing woody plant; slower to establish then increasingly vigorous.
uses: Large shady walls, pergolas, mature trees and vertical woodland gardens.
rootSize: Strong woody root system plus clinging aerial roots.
pollination: Fertile central flowers provide resources for pollinating insects.
uncertain: Taxonomy and accepted trade designation may differ between RHS and nursery labels.

hardinessNote: RHS H4 for variegated form; markedly less cold resilient than the green species. Best in sheltered southern/coastal gardens.
peak: Year-round foliage; insignificant flowers in spring
visual: Upright, bushy evergreen with glossy, leathery oval apple-green leaves edged irregularly in pale cream to ivory; forms a bright dense hedge.
pest: Generally pest free; rare leaf spot and honey fungus.
aspect: South or East in a sheltered, bright position, especially inland.
soil: Fertile, well-drained loam or sandy soil; flexible pH.
soilWarning: Exposed frosty, windy inland sites may burn or kill foliage. Avoid waterlogged winter soils.
water: Water weekly during establishment in dry periods; mature plants usually need watering only in prolonged drought.
prune: Clip hedges in late spring and again in late summer; remove browned or frost-damaged shoots after danger of hard frost.
toxicity: No major toxicity commonly reported, but ornamental foliage and berries are not food.
cvs: A variegated cultivar of New Zealand broadleaf, distinct from the greener, generally tougher species.
resilience: Tolerant of coastal conditions and wind once established in mild climates, but frost-sensitive inland.
uses: Variegated hedging, screens, bright evergreen structure and sheltered mixed borders.
pollination: Small yellow-green flowers usually insignificant; species is typically dioecious.
uncertain: Ultimate size often depends on clipping and UK winter exposure.

hardinessNote: RHS H3. Provide frost protection or movable containers outside mild UK coastal gardens.
visual: Bold upright to arching fans of strap-like bronze-green leaves dramatically edged and striped pink, crimson and red. Mature plants occasionally carry taller stems of tubular yellowish blooms.
pest: Phormium mealybug around leaf bases, occasional root damage and rare honey fungus.
aspect: Sunny sheltered South or West border; tolerates some light shade.
soil: Fertile, well-draining loam or sand; moderately moisture-retentive during growth.
soilWarning: Winter wet plus frost harms roots and crowns; strong freezing wind can scorch foliage.
water: Water well until established; established plants tolerate some drought, but containers need regular checks.
prune: Pull or cut dead, torn or frost-damaged leaves near their base in spring. Divide old clumps if required.
toxicity: Generally not listed as significantly toxic; sharp tough leaf edges may cut skin.
cvs: Phormium tenax Sundowner is also encountered under Phormium colensoi or generic Phormium trade naming.
resilience: Salt-wind tolerant in mild coastal sites; variable winter survival inland.
uses: Architectural focal points, coastal gardens, gravel planting and large tubs.
pollination: Rare flowers can attract nectar-feeding insects.
uncertain: Actual size and frost survival vary with microclimate and cultivar provenance.

hardinessNote: Species is a short-lived subshrub often grown as bedding; H4 is approximate and persistent winter wet reduces survival.
peak: Year-round silver foliage; yellow flowers Jun–Sep
visual: Compact silvery-white, felted foliage plant with deeply cut lobed leaves, creating high contrast with winter bedding; mature plants can bear yellow daisy-like flower heads.
pest: Usually pest resistant; occasional aphids and rust.
aspect: Bright South or West, sunny open situation.
soil: Poor to moderately fertile, sharply draining sandy, chalky or loamy soil.
soilWarning: Damp shade, heavy wet clay and winter saturation reduce foliage quality and survival.
water: Water at planting, then sparingly when established; tolerate drying better than waterlogging.
prune: Trim to retain compact foliage form and remove flower stalks if foliage display is the priority.
toxicity: Do not eat; related Jacobaea species contain potentially harmful compounds. Handle sensibly and restrict pet grazing.
cvs: Correct botanical name Jacobaea maritima; formerly Senecio maritimus / Senecio cineraria. Specific cultivar (e.g. Silver Dust) not identified.
resilience: Excellent tolerance of sun, salt spray, wind and short droughts; may be short lived in cold wet ground.
uses: Autumn and winter bedding, foliage edging, drought-tolerant containers, seaside beds and colour contrast.
foliage: evergreen to short-lived perennial, commonly grown as annual
rootSize: Fine to moderately fibrous root system.
pollination: Yellow flowers, when allowed, provide pollen and nectar to insects.
uncertain: Plants sold as Senecio maritima may refer to a distinct fine-cut cultivar; identification is to species only.
Exact toxicity profile of this taxon is not as well established as for some related Jacobaea species.

hardinessNote: Very cold hardy while dormant; above-ground growth naturally disappears in winter.
height: 15–25 cm foliage; flower stems to 30 cm
visual: Neat miniature mound of thick, almost round, cupped, blue-grey leaves resembling mouse ears; short stems hold lavender-purple bell-shaped flowers in summer.
pest: Slugs and snails; vine weevil in pots; occasional foliar nematodes or crown rot.
aspect: North or East; cool dappled or partial shade.
soil: Moist, humus-rich, free-draining loam with neutral to slightly acidic pH.
soilWarning: Hot sun scorches waxy blue foliage; prolonged drought damages leaves. Avoid persistently boggy compost.
water: Keep roots moist from spring growth through summer; water containers more frequently. Reduce watering in dormancy.
prune: Cut away spent flower spikes and remove yellow or collapsed leaves in late autumn; avoid damaging dormant buds.
toxicity: Toxic to dogs and cats if eaten; keep pets from chewing leaves or rhizomes.
cvs: A compact miniature hosta noted for thick foliage, though not completely slug-proof.
resilience: Extremely winter hardy; blue leaf bloom is best preserved out of direct afternoon sun.
uses: Shady pots, miniature woodland borders, rock gardens, path edges and troughs.
rootSize: Compact fleshy rhizomatous clump with fibrous roots.
pollination: Lavender flowers can attract bees and other pollinators.
uncertain: Flower stalk and leaf height vary by age and growing conditions.

hardinessNote: RHS H6; protect new shoots from late spring frost, cold winds and hot reflected sun.
visual: Slow-growing Japanese maple with rounded fan-shaped leaves often showing 11 shallow lobes; new leaves glow pale orange to chartreuse, turn fresh lime green and finish orange-red in autumn. Tiny purple-red spring flowers and red winged seeds.
pest: Aphids, scale insects and caterpillars; leaf scorch, Verticillium wilt and occasional honey fungus.
aspect: Sheltered East or West with morning or filtered light.
soil: Moisture-retentive but draining, humus-rich soil; prefers slightly acidic conditions but tolerates neutral and some alkaline soils.
soilWarning: Avoid desiccating wind, hot afternoon sun, standing water and drought in pots.
water: Keep newly planted specimens evenly moist; deeply water containers and soil during hot dry spells.
prune: Minimal shaping in late autumn or winter while dormant; remove crossing or dead shoots.
toxicity: Not generally listed as significantly toxic; ornamental seeds are not for food.
cvs: Also sometimes listed as Acer japonicum Jordan; RHS accepted name is Acer shirasawanum Jordan.
resilience: Winter hardy but foliage sensitive to wind and scorch.
uses: Specimen tree, shaded courtyard, Japanese garden, large patio container.
rootSize: Shallow to intermediate fibrous roots, eventually broad.
pollination: Spring flowers are small but usable by visiting insects.
uncertain: Summer foliage shade varies with climate, shade and age.

hardinessNote: RHS H6 but young growth and foliage can be damaged by late frost or desiccating wind.
peak: Apr–May spring colour; Oct–Nov autumn colour
visual: Architectural Japanese maple with deeply divided, narrow, seven-lobed leaves whose margins curl under. Foliage starts deep burgundy-purple, may bronze or green somewhat in summer and flashes orange-red in autumn.
pest: Aphids, scale, caterpillars and gall mites; risk of leaf scorch and Verticillium wilt.
aspect: Sheltered East, West or bright South with protection from harsh midday sun.
soil: Fertile, moist but well-drained soil, ideally slightly acidic to neutral.
soilWarning: Leaf edges scorch if roots dry out or if exposed to hot sun and wind.
water: Water deeply in dry weather and regularly in containers, while allowing drainage.
prune: Only lightly prune during dormancy in late autumn or winter.
toxicity: Not recognised as significantly poisonous under ordinary garden use.
cvs: Matsumurae group cultivar, distinctly red-purple and different from Green Trompenburg.
resilience: Hardy woody framework, with ornamental leaves that need a sheltered microclimate.
uses: Japanese planting, focal tree, large tubs and contrasting foliage borders.
rootSize: Shallow fibrous roots, expanding with age.
stockForm: Upright rounded small tree or large shrub.
pollination: Small spring flowers visited by some insects; winged seeds follow.
uncertain: RHS records a smaller mature stature than some nursery estimates for older specimens.

hardinessNote: RHS H6; sheltered locations maintain foliage quality.
visual: Upright Japanese maple with large, deeply cut green leaves and unusual curled-under lobe margins. Emerges lime green with red-tinted edges before becoming green, then yellow to orange in autumn.
pest: Aphids, scale insects and caterpillars; Verticillium wilt, scorch and occasional honey fungus.
aspect: Sheltered East, West or light South; filtered light or gentle sun.
soil: Fertile, moisture-retentive but well-drained acid to neutral loam; improved clay can work.
soilWarning: Avoid hot dry wind, deep stagnant winter water and severe summer drought.
water: Maintain moisture during establishment and during hot spells, especially in pots.
prune: Very little pruning; tidy in late autumn to midwinter while dormant.
toxicity: No significant poisoning risk typically cited for ornamental Acer palmatum.
cvs: Correct cultivar spelling Green Trompenburg (not Trompenberg); green-leaved relative distinct from red Trompenburg.
resilience: Cold-hardy tree with potentially scorch-prone foliage during summer drought.
uses: Courtyard specimens, woodland edges, Japanese-style gardens and large borders.
rootSize: Broadening fibrous woody roots; avoid excessive drying.
pollination: Small spring flowers may support insects; winged fruits produced.
uncertain: Allow substantial long-term room; RHS mature height up to 8 m.

common: Lampranthus / trailing ice plant (identity to confirm)
hardinessNote: Species unidentified. Similar Lampranthus are commonly frost tender and should be overwintered frost-free in most UK gardens.
visual: Likely a mat-forming succulent with narrow fleshy triangular leaves and abundant sun-opening, daisy-like flowers in bright pink, purple, red, orange or yellow. Actual colour and habit must be checked against the label.
pest: Aphids, mealybugs; root rot if watered heavily or kept cold and wet.
aspect: Full sun on a warm South or West terrace; winter under bright frost-free cover.
soil: Very free-draining cactus mix, sandy soil or gravel; pH adaptable.
soilWarning: Keep away from frosts and saturated winter compost; flowers may remain closed in dull light.
water: Water moderately while actively growing, then let the surface dry. Keep sparingly watered and frost-free over winter.
prune: Pinch overlong stems and remove damaged shoots in spring; root healthy cuttings if needed.
toxicity: Not established for unidentified species; do not eat and do not assume pet safety.
cvs: Input Lamaranthus Mesembrianthemum Algarve Portugal interpreted cautiously as Lampranthus sp. / mesembryanthemum-type ice plant. Algarve Portugal is not verified as a cultivar name.
resilience: Excellent sun and drought tolerance; poor frost and winter-wet resistance.
uses: Sunny patio tubs, rock gardens in frost-free climates, hanging planters and summer bedding.
pollination: Open flowers can attract bees and other insects in full sun.
uncertain: ESSENTIAL: Lamaranthus is likely a misspelling, and Mesembrianthemum is applied loosely to several Aizoaceae genera.
Algarve Portugal could be origin or label branding, not a botanical cultivar.
Species, flower colour, size, hardiness and bloom season cannot be verified without label/photo.

hardiness: Breeder claim: to about −12°C (roughly H5 range, not a verified RHS rating)
hardinessNote: Plantipp lists frost tolerance to −12°C. Actual survival in UK winter depends heavily on maturity, site and drainage; shelter from cold wind.
visual: Compact upright evergreen with glossy dark green leaves and large, intensely fragrant, many-petalled double white flowers, sometimes ageing cream.
pest: Scale, aphids, mealybugs and spider mite; chlorosis, bud drop and root rot when conditions are unsuitable.
aspect: Sheltered East, West or bright South with morning sun and protection from scorching afternoon heat.
soil: Humus-rich, moist but freely draining acidic soil, ideally around pH 5–6.
soilWarning: Lime-rich soils or alkaline water cause yellowing; avoid cold soggy roots, severe frost exposure and drying during bud formation.
water: Keep evenly moist with rainwater when possible; do not leave standing in water. Feed acid-loving plants during active growth.
prune: Lightly shape straight after flowering; remove damaged wood when spring regrowth begins.
toxicity: Not generally classified as severely toxic to humans; ingestion can upset pets, so discourage chewing and eating.
cvs: Double Diamonds is the selling name, 'Leefour' is the cultivar denomination (PBR).
resilience: Breeder reports superior heat and disease tolerance for a gardenia; protect against frost extremes in the UK.
uses: Fragrant patio container, doorway, sheltered acidic borders and conservatory displays.
rootSize: Compact fibrous woody root ball; dislikes extreme water swings.
pollination: Fully double flowers may offer less pollen accessibility than single-flowered gardenias.
uncertain: Breeder −12°C hardiness is not the same as an officially assigned RHS cultivar hardiness rating.
Bloom timing varies widely with overwintering temperature and growing conditions.
